lessons.title: CPU, Main Memory and the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
lessons.description: Von Neumann model, CPU components, three buses and the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
lessons.content_html:
The Von Neumann Stored-Program Concept

Every computer you have used — from a school laptop to a smartphone — runs on the same fundamental idea: both the program instructions and the data those instructions act on are stored together in the same memory. This is the von Neumann stored-program concept, named after the mathematician John von Neumann, whose work in the 1940s described this model. Before this idea took hold, changing what a computer did meant physically rewiring it. The stored-program concept meant you could change a program simply by changing the data in memory — the same hardware could run any program.

Main memory (RAM) is where instructions and data live while the computer is running. The CPU reads instructions from RAM, processes them, and writes results back. Because RAM is directly accessible by the CPU, it is far faster than any secondary storage device. However, RAM is volatile — everything in it disappears when the power is switched off.

Key Fact

The von Neumann model has five key CPU components: the control unit, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), registers, the clock, and the three buses (address, data, control). The CPU works directly with main memory (RAM). Every instruction the CPU executes was stored in RAM as data.

Inside the CPU: Components and Their Roles

The control unit does not process data itself. Instead, it orchestrates everything else — sending signals to tell the ALU to calculate, instructing memory to send data, and directing results to the correct destination. During the fetch-decode-execute cycle, the control unit is in charge of every stage.

The ALU is where all computation happens. Arithmetic operations include addition and subtraction. Logical operations include comparisons between values and Boolean operations. Every time a program checks a condition (is the score greater than 50?) or performs a calculation (total price × quantity), the ALU is doing the work.

Registers are tiny storage areas on the processor chip itself. Because they are physically part of the CPU, they can be accessed far faster than RAM. They hold the data that the CPU is working with right now — for example, the result of the last calculation or the address of the next instruction to fetch. You do not need to know the names of specific registers for your exam.

The clock generates a continuous stream of electrical pulses. Each pulse can trigger the start of a new stage in the fetch-decode-execute cycle. The faster the clock, the more stages the CPU can complete per second. A modern CPU typically operates at several gigahertz (GHz) — billions of pulses per second.

A bus is a collection of parallel wires. The CPU communicates with RAM (and other components) via three buses, each carrying a different type of signal:

Address bus — carries the memory address the CPU wants to read from or write to. It is one-directional: the CPU sends addresses out, but nothing sends addresses back to the CPU. The number of address lines determines how many distinct memory locations the CPU can access.

Data bus — carries the actual data or instruction being transferred. It is bidirectional: data travels from RAM to the CPU during a fetch, and from the CPU back to RAM when the CPU writes a result.

Control bus — carries control signals that coordinate the activity of all components. For example, it carries a signal telling RAM whether the current operation is a read (fetch data) or a write (store data). Without the control bus, components would not know when to act or in what direction data should flow.

Together, the three buses make up the system bus — the communication highway between the CPU and main memory.

The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle

The CPU operates by endlessly repeating a three-stage process for every instruction in a program. This is the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Each instruction is processed in strict sequence: fetch, then decode, then execute.

Stage 1 — Fetch: The CPU needs to know which instruction to get. It places the address of the next instruction on the address bus. RAM responds by placing the instruction on the data bus. The control bus carries a “read” signal telling RAM that this is a fetch operation, not a write. The instruction arrives at the CPU and is held in a register ready for the next stage.

Stage 2 — Decode: The control unit examines the instruction and works out what operation is required. Different instructions mean different things — one might mean “add two numbers”, another might mean “move data to a different memory location”. The control unit figures out which components need to act and what data they need. No data moves along the buses during decode; this stage happens entirely inside the CPU.

Stage 3 — Execute: The instruction is carried out. If it is an arithmetic operation, the ALU performs the calculation. If data needs to be written to RAM, the CPU places the destination address on the address bus, the data on the data bus, and sends a “write” signal on the control bus. Once execution is complete, the cycle immediately begins again for the next instruction.

This cycle repeats billions of times per second. A common exam error is writing only two stages (“fetch and execute”). There are always three stages: fetch, decode and execute. Omitting decode loses a mark.

Key Fact

During Fetch: the address bus carries the address; the data bus carries the instruction back; the control bus signals a read. During Decode: the control unit interprets the instruction — no bus activity needed. During Execute: the ALU or memory handles the operation; the data bus may carry a result back to RAM via a write signal on the control bus.

Putting It Together: A Worked Example

Imagine a simple program instruction: “Add the value stored at memory address 50 to the value stored at memory address 51 and store the result at address 52.”

Fetch: The address of this instruction (say, address 10) goes out on the address bus. RAM sends the instruction back on the data bus. The control bus signals “read”.

Decode: The control unit reads the instruction. It identifies this as an “add” operation needing two source addresses (50 and 51) and a destination (52). It prepares the ALU.

Execute: The CPU fetches the value at address 50 (using the address bus and data bus), then fetches the value at address 51. The ALU adds them together. The result is placed on the data bus; address 52 goes on the address bus; the control bus signals “write”. RAM stores the result. Cycle complete — on to the next instruction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Your exam will test the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle often, sometimes as a 4-mark ‘Describe’ question. Always write all three stages by name and describe what happens in each. Never compress it to ‘fetch and execute’ — examiners look for ‘decode’ as a separate stage. When a question mentions ‘buses’, be specific: name which bus (address, data, or control) and what it carries for that particular step. If asked to ‘Explain’, add the consequence: e.g. “the instruction is placed on the data bus so it can travel from RAM to the CPU.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The von Neumann stored-program concept means both instructions and data are held together in the same main memory (RAM), allowing the CPU to execute any program stored there.
  • The CPU contains the control unit (manages the cycle), ALU (performs calculations and comparisons), registers (fast on-chip storage), and clock (generates timing pulses). Three buses (address, data, control) connect the CPU to RAM.
  • The fetch-decode-execute cycle has exactly three stages: fetch the instruction from RAM using the buses, decode it in the control unit, then execute it (ALU or memory write). This repeats for every instruction, billions of times per second.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the control unit in the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The control unit manages and coordinates the entire fetch-decode-execute cycle. It sends signals to RAM via the control bus to indicate whether the operation is a read or write. During the decode stage, it interprets the instruction to determine which components must act and what data they need. It then directs the ALU, registers and memory accordingly during execute.
Secure: States the control unit manages the cycle and decodes instructions, with some reference to directing other components.
Developing: States the control unit manages the CPU or decodes instructions, but lacks supporting detail.
Emerging: Vague reference to the control unit being involved in processing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of the address bus during the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During fetch, the CPU places the address of the next instruction on the address bus. The address bus carries this address to RAM so RAM knows which memory location to access. The address bus is one-directional (CPU to RAM). This allows the correct instruction to be located and placed on the data bus to travel back to the CPU.
Secure: States that the address bus carries the address of the instruction to RAM, with some explanation of why this is needed.
Developing: States the address bus is used during fetch but does not explain its direction or purpose clearly.
Emerging: Names the address bus without explaining its role.

practice_questions.text: State the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all three correct and in order: fetch, decode, execute.

practice_questions.text: Name the component of the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical operations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: ALU (accept: arithmetic logic unit).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the decode stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: the control unit (1 mark) examines or interprets the instruction to determine what operation is needed and which components must act / what data is required (1 mark). Accept references to the control unit identifying the operation type. No bus activity is required during decode.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether increasing clock speed is always the best way to improve CPU performance. Consider the role of the clock and other factors that affect performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that a higher clock speed means more fetch-decode-execute cycles per second, improving throughput. However, increasing clock speed alone has diminishing returns: it generates more heat, can cause stability issues, and the CPU may still be bottlenecked by RAM access speeds (the bus transfers data at a fixed rate regardless of clock speed). Other factors also affect performance — for example, the number of cores allows parallel processing of independent tasks, and larger on-chip cache reduces the frequency of slow RAM accesses. Concludes that clock speed is one of several factors; the best improvement depends on the workload.
Secure: Identifies clock speed as increasing cycles per second, notes at least one limitation, and mentions one other performance factor (e.g. cores or cache) with some explanation.
Developing: Explains that faster clock means more operations per second; mentions one other factor without development.
Emerging: States clock speed affects performance; little or no development.

glossary_terms.definition: A computer architecture in which program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory, and the CPU fetches and executes instructions one at a time.
Volatile primary storage that holds program instructions and data currently being used by the CPU. Contents are lost when power is removed.
The part of the CPU that manages and coordinates all activity, directing data between components and controlling the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Arithmetic Logic Unit — the part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic operations and logical comparisons.
Small, extremely fast storage locations built directly into the CPU. They temporarily hold data, addresses and instructions that the CPU is currently working with.
A component that generates regular electrical pulses to synchronise the activities of the CPU. Clock speed is measured in hertz (Hz).
A set of parallel wires along which binary signals are transmitted between the CPU and other components. Different buses carry different types of information.
The continuous three-stage process by which the CPU processes instructions: fetch (retrieve from RAM), decode (interpret the instruction) and execute (carry it out).

lessons.title: Secondary Storage and Embedded Systems
lessons.description: Magnetic, optical and solid-state storage compared, plus what makes a system embedded.
lessons.content_html:
Why Is Secondary Storage Needed?

Main memory (RAM) is fast and directly accessible by the CPU, but it has a critical weakness: it is volatile. Switch the computer off and everything in RAM disappears. This is why computers also need secondary storage — a separate, permanent place to keep files, applications and the operating system itself.

Secondary storage provides three things that RAM cannot: persistence (data survives when the power is off), capacity (far more data can be held — measured in tebibytes (TiB)) and portability (storage devices can be moved between computers). The CPU cannot access secondary storage directly — data must first be copied into RAM before the processor can work with it.

Key Fact

Secondary storage is needed because RAM is volatile. It provides persistence (data retained without power), capacity (far more storage than RAM — modern drives hold multiple tebibytes) and portability (devices can be transported and plugged into other systems). The CPU must load data from secondary storage into RAM before it can process it.

Magnetic Storage

Magnetic storage encodes data using magnetic fields. In a hard disk drive (HDD), one or more metal platters spin at high speed, coated with a magnetic material. A read/write head floats just above the surface, magnetising tiny regions to record 0s and 1s. To read data, the head detects the magnetic orientation of each region as the platter spins past.

HDDs offer high capacity at relatively low cost per gibibyte — making them popular for desktop computers and large-scale data storage. However, because mechanical parts must physically move to the right position, access times are slower than solid-state alternatives. HDDs are also vulnerable to physical shock: a jolt while the drive is spinning can damage the head or platters.

Optical Storage

Optical storage uses a laser to read and write data. The surface of a disc contains millions of microscopic pits and flat areas (called lands); the laser bounces off these differently, and the detector interprets the pattern as 0s and 1s. Common optical formats are:

  • CD — typically around 700 mebibytes (MiB) capacity. Used for audio and small data files.
  • DVD — typically 4.7 to 8.5 gibibytes (GiB). Used for films and software distribution.
  • Blu-ray — typically 25 to 50 GiB or more per disc. Used for high-definition video and large data archives.

Optical discs are robust and cheap to manufacture in bulk, making them good for distributing content. However, capacity per disc is limited compared to HDDs or SSDs, and they can be scratched or damaged.

Solid-State Storage

Solid-state storage (SSD) holds data in electronic memory chips. Because there are no spinning platters or moving heads, SSDs are considerably faster than HDDs — a file that takes several seconds to open from an HDD may open almost instantly from an SSD. They are also silent, use less power, and are far more resistant to physical shock.

The main disadvantage of SSDs is cost: they are more expensive per gibibyte of capacity than HDDs. However, prices have fallen significantly, and SSDs are now the standard in laptops, tablets and smartphones.

Magnetic (HDD): High capacity at low cost per GiB — HDDs are still cheaper per GiB than SSDs. Slower access due to mechanical movement. Vulnerable to physical shock. Produces some noise and heat. Good for large-capacity desktop storage or data centres where cost matters more than speed.

Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): Low cost to produce in bulk. Portable and can be read on any compatible drive. Limited capacity per disc. Slow to write. Prone to surface scratches. Best suited for distributing content or long-term archival where the discs are not frequently written to.

Solid-state (SSD): Fast access and data transfer. No moving parts — silent, light and shock-resistant. Lower power consumption. More expensive per GiB than HDD. Best for laptops, mobile devices and applications where speed and durability matter (e.g. gaming, video editing on the go).

Key Fact

The key trade-off: magnetic (HDD) gives the most capacity for the lowest price but is slow and fragile. Optical is cheap to manufacture and portable but limited in capacity. Solid-state (SSD) is fastest and most durable but costs more per gibibyte. Exam questions often ask you to justify a choice for a specific scenario — match the storage type to the use case.

Embedded Systems

Most computers are general-purpose: you can install any software and use them for many different tasks. An embedded system is different. It is a computer (with a processor, memory and software) built inside a larger product to control a specific function. The user cannot install new programs on it — it does its one job, repeatedly, for the life of the product.

Embedded systems are everywhere. A washing machine contains an embedded system that controls the water temperature, drum speed and cycle timing. A smart thermostat uses an embedded processor to monitor temperature sensors and switch heating on or off. A car’s engine control unit (ECU) is an embedded system that reads sensor data from the engine dozens of times per second and adjusts fuel injection, ignition timing and other variables in real time.

Because an embedded system has a fixed purpose, it can be optimised in ways a general-purpose computer cannot. The processor can be smaller and cheaper. The software is stored in read-only or flash memory and starts running the moment power is applied — no operating system needs to “boot up” in the way a desktop PC does. The system only needs enough memory and processing power for its specific task, keeping cost and energy consumption low.

Reliability is critical for embedded systems. A washing machine controller that crashes mid-cycle is a serious problem; a car’s ECU failing at speed could be dangerous. Embedded software is therefore typically simpler and more rigorously tested than general-purpose software, with fewer features and less opportunity for unexpected states.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Storage questions often ask you to ‘Explain’ which storage type is most suitable for a scenario. Always link your choice to a specific advantage and justify it: don’t just say “SSD is fast” — say “SSD has no moving parts so data is accessed faster, which is important for a laptop that needs to open files quickly on battery power.” For embedded systems, examiners want to see that you understand the fixed-purpose nature: state that the device performs “one specific function” and that the user cannot install new programs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Secondary storage is needed because RAM is volatile. It provides persistence, capacity and portability. The three types are magnetic (HDD — high capacity, low cost, mechanical), optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray — cheap to produce, portable, limited capacity) and solid-state (SSD — fast, durable, no moving parts, more expensive per GiB).
  • An embedded system is a computer built into a device to perform one specific function continuously. Examples include washing machine controllers, smart thermostats and engine control units. Users cannot install new programs on an embedded system.

practice_questions.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of solid-state storage compared to magnetic hard disk storage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for advantage: no moving parts so faster access / more durable / lighter / uses less power / silent. 1 mark for disadvantage: more expensive per GiB / lower maximum capacity available for the same price.

practice_questions.text: Explain why secondary storage is needed in a computer system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: RAM is volatile — all data is lost when power is removed, so secondary storage is required to retain files, programs and the operating system permanently. Secondary storage also provides far greater capacity than RAM (multiple TiB vs typically 8–32 GiB of RAM) and can be portable, allowing data to be moved between systems. Mentions that the CPU cannot access secondary storage directly — data must be loaded into RAM first.
Secure: States that secondary storage retains data without power (persistence) and gives one other reason (capacity or portability) with explanation.
Developing: States that secondary storage keeps data when the computer is off, no further development.
Emerging: Vague reference to saving files.

practice_questions.text: Define the term embedded system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: a computer system (processor + memory + software) (1 mark) built into a larger device to perform one specific function, which users cannot reprogram (1 mark). Accept examples that illustrate the fixed-purpose nature.

practice_questions.text: A school is setting up a new IT suite. The head of department suggests using HDDs for the computers because they are cheaper than SSDs. Discuss whether HDDs are the most suitable storage for this use case.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: HDDs offer high capacity at lower cost per GiB, which is relevant for a school budget. However, HDDs are mechanical and slower — boot times and file access will be noticeably slower than SSDs, which may affect lesson time and student experience. SSDs are more durable (no moving parts), important in an environment where computers may be knocked. SSDs also use less power. However, if cost is the primary constraint, HDDs may be acceptable if speed is not critical. Conclusion: the decision depends on budget vs performance priorities; a mixed approach (SSD for the boot drive, HDD for bulk storage) could optimise both.
Secure: Identifies cost advantage of HDD and speed advantage of SSD; makes a reasoned recommendation with reference to the school context.
Developing: Contrasts HDD and SSD on one or two features with limited connection to the scenario.
Emerging: Simple statements about HDDs or SSDs without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Give one example of an embedded system and describe what it does.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid example (washing machine controller, engine control unit, smart thermostat, microwave controller, traffic light controller, etc.). 1 mark for describing its function in terms of monitoring input and controlling a specific output or process.

practice_questions.text: Identify which storage type — magnetic, optical or solid-state — would be most suitable for archiving large amounts of data at the lowest cost, and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnetic (HDD) offers the highest capacity at the lowest cost per GiB, making it the most cost-effective choice for archiving large data volumes. The access speed of HDDs is less critical for archival use (data is read infrequently). Mentions that HDDs are more cost-effective than SSDs and have higher capacity per unit than optical media, which would require many discs for large archives.
Secure: Identifies HDD or magnetic storage and gives cost per GiB as the reason; some comparison with at least one other type.
Developing: Identifies a storage type with a relevant reason but no comparison.
Emerging: Names a storage type without explanation.

glossary_terms.definition: Memory that loses all its stored data when the power supply is switched off.
Persistent storage separate from main memory, used to hold files, programs and the operating system when the computer is not actively processing them.
A unit of data storage equal to 1024 gibibytes. Edexcel uses binary multiples (1024-based): 1 TiB = 1024 GiB = 1024 × 1024 MiB = 1024 × 1024 × 1024 KiB = 1024⁴ bytes.
A storage technology that encodes data as magnetic fields on a surface. Hard disk drives use spinning platters and a moving read/write head.
A storage technology that uses a laser to read and write data encoded as pits and lands on a spinning disc. Examples include CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs.
A storage technology that uses electronic flash memory chips with no moving parts. Data is stored as electrical charges in floating-gate transistors.
A computer system built into a larger device and designed to perform one or a small set of specific functions. The user cannot install new programs on it.

lessons.title: Operating Systems, Utility Software and Robust Software
lessons.description: OS functions, utility programs, and audit trails and code reviews for robust software.
lessons.content_html:
What Is an Operating System?

Every computer needs a layer of software that manages its hardware resources and provides a platform on which applications can run. This is the operating system (OS). Without an OS, every application would need to contain its own code to communicate with hardware — an impossible duplication of effort. Instead, applications request services from the OS, and the OS handles the low-level work.

Your exam requires you to know four specific functions of an operating system: file management, process management, peripheral management and user management. Each addresses a different aspect of running a computer system reliably.

Key Fact

The four OS functions you must know: File management (organising, storing and retrieving files), Process management (deciding which programs get CPU time and when), Peripheral management (handling communication with input/output devices), User management (creating accounts, setting permissions and controlling access).

The Four OS Functions in Detail

File management keeps track of where every file is stored on secondary storage. The OS maintains a directory structure (folders within folders), tracks file names, sizes and locations, and enforces access permissions (who is allowed to read or modify a file). When you save a document, the OS decides where on the storage device to place it and updates its records.

Process management handles multiple programs running at the same time. A modern computer might have dozens of processes active — the browser, the music player, the background virus scan. The OS switches the CPU between them so quickly that they all appear to run simultaneously. It also manages what happens when a process needs to wait (e.g. for a file to load) — pausing that process and giving the CPU to something else.

Peripheral management allows the CPU to communicate with hardware devices such as printers, keyboards, screens and storage devices. Because each device is different, the OS uses a device driver — a small program that translates between the OS’s standard instructions and the specific commands a particular device understands. When you plug in a new printer, the OS loads or downloads the appropriate driver.

User management allows different people to use the same computer with separate settings and access rights. A school network, for example, might allow students to save files only in their own folder and block access to system settings, while giving network administrators full control. Each user has an account with a defined set of permissions.

Utility Software

Utility software carries out maintenance tasks. Unlike application software (which helps users complete their own work), utility programs serve the system itself. The five utility types on your specification are file repair, backup, data compression, disk defragmentation and anti-malware.

File repair — attempts to recover files that have become corrupted or unreadable. This can happen if a drive develops bad sectors, a file is partially overwritten, or a program crashes mid-save. A file repair utility scans for corruption and rebuilds as much of the file as possible.

Backup utility — creates copies of files and stores them in a secondary location (another drive, a network server, or an external device). If the original files are lost or corrupted, they can be restored from the backup. Backup utilities can be scheduled to run automatically so that copies are kept up to date.

Data compression utility — reduces the size of files so they take up less storage space or can be transferred more quickly. Some compression is lossless (the original can be perfectly reconstructed); other compression is lossy (some quality is permanently discarded). A file archiver (such as a ZIP tool) is a common example of lossless compression utility software.

Disk defragmentation — reorganises files on a magnetic hard disk. Over time, as files are added, deleted and modified, their data becomes fragmented — scattered in non-contiguous sections across the disk surface. A defragmenter moves fragments together so the read/write head needs to travel less, speeding up file access. Note: SSDs do not benefit from defragmentation (and it can reduce their lifespan), so this utility applies to magnetic HDDs only.

Anti-malware — detects, quarantines and removes malicious software (malware) such as viruses, spyware and ransomware. It does this by scanning files against a database of known malware signatures, or by monitoring for suspicious behaviour. Anti-malware is a utility because it maintains the health and security of the system rather than performing a user task.

Robust Software: Why It Matters

Robust software is software that continues to work correctly even when things do not go as planned — unexpected inputs, high traffic, or deliberate attempts to exploit a weakness. In safety-critical systems (medical devices, banking, aircraft control), a software failure can have serious real-world consequences. Even in everyday applications, a crash or a vulnerability that leaks user data is costly.

Developing robust software requires identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. Two methods the specification requires you to know are audit trails and code reviews.

A code review is a design-time technique. Before the software is released, one or more developers read through the source code written by a colleague, looking for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses and poor practices. A fresh pair of eyes often catches vulnerabilities the original developer missed. Code reviews are particularly effective at identifying issues such as missing input validation (which could allow malicious data to crash the program) or hardcoded passwords.

An audit trail is a run-time technique. While the software is in use, it automatically records a timestamped log of significant actions: which user logged in, which files were accessed, what data was changed and when. If a security incident occurs — say, a database record is altered without authorisation — the audit trail provides a record of what happened, when, and under which account. This makes it possible to trace breaches and investigate suspicious activity.

The key distinction: a code review happens before the software runs (during development) and aims to prevent vulnerabilities from shipping. An audit trail happens while the software runs (at runtime) and aims to detect and trace problems after they occur.

Key Fact

A code review is a design-time technique: developers read each other’s source code before release to find bugs and security weaknesses. An audit trail is a run-time technique: the system automatically logs who did what and when, so security breaches can be traced. Code reviews prevent problems; audit trails detect and record them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing OS functions, use precise language — ‘file management’ is not the same as ‘managing the CPU’. Exam questions often give a scenario and ask you to ‘Explain’ which OS function is involved: match the scenario to exactly one of the four functions. For robust software, the key distinction examiners test is design-time vs run-time: code review happens before the software is released; an audit trail runs while the software is live. Always include both the what and the why — don’t just name audit trail, say “it logs user actions so that security breaches can be detected and traced.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An operating system manages four areas: file management (organising files), process management (allocating CPU time), peripheral management (communicating with devices via drivers) and user management (accounts and permissions).
  • Utility software maintains the system: file repair, backup, data compression, disk defragmentation (HDDs only) and anti-malware are the five types required by the specification.
  • Robust software resists failure and exploits. Code reviews (design-time: developers inspect code before release) and audit trails (run-time: automatic logs of who did what and when) are two methods for identifying and tracking vulnerabilities.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a code review helps developers create more robust software.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review involves one or more developers reading through code written by a colleague before it is released. The reviewer looks for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses (e.g. missing input validation, hardcoded credentials) and poor coding practices. Because the reviewer did not write the code, they approach it with fresh eyes and can spot issues the original developer overlooked. Identifying vulnerabilities at design time means they can be fixed before users are exposed to them, making the software safer and more reliable.

Developing: States that a code review involves checking code for errors, without explaining the mechanism or benefit.
Emerging: Vague reference to checking code.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of an audit trail in a software system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: an audit trail is an automatic log (1 mark) that records who performed each action, what was changed, and when, so that security incidents or unauthorised access can be traced or detected (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain one difference between a code review and an audit trail as methods of making software more robust.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review is a design-time technique carried out before the software is released: developers inspect source code to find and fix vulnerabilities before users encounter them. An audit trail is a run-time technique that operates while the software is live: it logs actions automatically so that if something goes wrong (e.g. a data breach), there is a record of what happened and when. The key difference is timing and purpose: code review prevents problems from shipping; audit trails detect and allow investigation of problems after they occur.
Secure: Identifies that one is before release and one operates during use, with some explanation of each.
Developing: Names both techniques and states one difference without development.
Emerging: Names both techniques with no difference stated.

practice_questions.text: Identify which utility program a system administrator would use if files on a magnetic hard disk were taking much longer to open than usual, and explain why this utility would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Disk defragmentation. Over time, files on a magnetic HDD become fragmented — their data is split across non-contiguous sectors of the platter. When a file is opened, the read/write head must physically move to each fragment in turn, increasing access time. Defragmentation reorganises the file data so it is stored in contiguous sectors, meaning the head travels less distance and access is faster. Notes that defragmentation applies to HDDs, not SSDs.
Secure: Identifies defragmentation and explains that fragmented files cause the head to move more, slowing access.
Developing: Identifies defragmentation without a full explanation of why fragmentation causes slowness.
Emerging: Names a utility but incorrect or no explanation.

glossary_terms.definition: A type of system software that manages hardware resources and provides services for application software, handling file, process, peripheral and user management.
An OS function that organises files into a directory structure, controls access permissions, and manages reading and writing to storage.
An OS function that manages which programs are running, allocates CPU time between them, and switches between processes so the computer appears to run multiple programs simultaneously.
An OS function that manages communication between the computer and its input and output devices, using device drivers to translate between the OS and specific hardware.
An OS function that creates and manages user accounts, sets access permissions, and controls what each user is allowed to do on the system.
Software that performs maintenance or support tasks for the computer system rather than directly serving the end user's primary work.
Software that operates reliably and correctly under a wide range of conditions, including unexpected inputs, high load and attempts to exploit vulnerabilities.
A chronological log of events automatically recorded by a system, capturing who performed each action, what was changed, and when — used to detect and investigate security incidents.
A design-time technique in which developers read through each other's source code before release to find bugs, logic errors and security weaknesses.

lessons.title: Programming Languages: High-level, Low-level, Compilers and Interpreters
lessons.description: High- and low-level languages compared, and how compilers and interpreters work.
lessons.content_html:
Why Programming Languages Exist

A processor can only execute instructions written in machine code — binary patterns of 0s and 1s. Writing programs directly in machine code is extraordinarily difficult: a single instruction such as “add the value in register A to register B” becomes a long binary string, and the programmer must track every memory address manually. Programming languages were invented to give developers a more readable and manageable way to express instructions, which must then be translated into machine code before the processor can run them.

Low-Level Languages

Low-level languages are close to the hardware. They map almost directly onto the processor’s instruction set. Two types are relevant to your exam:

Machine code is the only language a processor can execute directly. It consists entirely of binary and is specific to a processor family — code written for one architecture will not run on a different one without modification.

Assembly language replaces raw binary with short, human-readable codes called mnemonics (for example, MOV to move data between locations, ADD to add two values, SUB to subtract). Each mnemonic maps directly to exactly one machine code instruction — this is called a one-to-one correspondence. Assembly language is still tightly bound to a specific processor’s instruction set. It is used when a developer needs precise control over hardware, such as in firmware or embedded systems.

Key Fact

Low-level languages give precise hardware control and produce fast, memory-efficient programs — because the programmer decides exactly what the processor does. The disadvantages are that they are hard to read and write, processor-specific (not portable to different hardware), and take much longer to develop in than high-level alternatives.

High-Level Languages

High-level languages use syntax that resembles natural language — words like print, if, while and return. One high-level instruction often corresponds to many machine code instructions, so much more is achieved with fewer lines of code. Python 3, the language assessed in the practical paper, is a high-level language.

High-level languages are portable: the same Python program can run on a Windows PC, a Mac and a Linux server without modification — as long as the appropriate Python interpreter is installed. This is possible because the language abstracts away the hardware details; translation to machine code is handled by a compiler or interpreter for each platform.

High-level languages are also much easier to debug. Meaningful variable names, structured control flow and comments make programs readable to any developer familiar with the language, not just the original author. This reduces the time needed to find and fix errors.

Readability: High-level uses English-like keywords; low-level uses binary or mnemonics — much harder to interpret at a glance.

Portability: High-level programs can run on different hardware (with a suitable translator); low-level programs are tied to a specific processor instruction set.

Hardware control: Low-level gives precise control over every CPU register and memory address; high-level abstracts these details away.

Development speed: High-level is far faster to write and debug; low-level requires understanding of the processor architecture and is error-prone.

Execution efficiency: Low-level programs can be more memory-efficient and faster when optimised by a skilled programmer; high-level programs rely on the translator to produce efficient machine code.

Translators: Compilers and Interpreters

Because processors only understand machine code, programs written in high-level languages must be translated. There are two main types of translator: the compiler and the interpreter.

A compiler reads the entire source code of a program and translates it all into machine code at once, before the program runs. The output is a standalone executable file. Once compiled, the program can be distributed and run on any compatible machine without the compiler being present. Errors are reported after the whole program has been analysed — the compiler lists all the problems it found, so the developer can fix them together before re-compiling.

An interpreter translates and executes the program one statement at a time. It does not produce a machine code file; instead, it translates each statement and immediately runs it. If an error is encountered, execution stops at that line — making it immediately clear where the problem is. The interpreter must be present every time the program runs, and execution is generally slower because translation happens at run time rather than beforehand.

Imagine a Python program with 200 lines. There is a bug on line 150.

With an interpreter: The program runs fine for the first 149 lines. When the interpreter reaches line 150, it stops and reports the error. The developer fixes line 150 and runs again. This makes finding the error easy — the interpreter shows exactly which line failed.

With a compiler: The compiler analyses all 200 lines before running anything. It reports all errors it finds (including line 150). The developer fixes every error, then compiles again. Once compiled successfully, the resulting executable runs quickly on any compatible machine — no Python interpreter is needed to run it.

Developers often use an interpreter during development (fast feedback, line-by-line error location) and compile for the final product (faster execution, no dependency on the interpreter).

Key Fact

Compiler: translates the whole program before execution, produces a standalone machine code executable, reports errors after analysing the whole program, runs faster (no run-time translation needed). Interpreter: translates one statement at a time during execution, produces no standalone executable (interpreter must always be present), stops at the first error (easier to locate), runs slower.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common exam question on translators is a ‘Describe’ or ‘Explain’ comparing compiler and interpreter. Examiners look for three dimensions: when translation happens (all at once before execution vs line-by-line during execution), what output is produced (standalone executable vs no file), and how errors are handled (all errors listed after analysis vs stops at first error). Don’t just say “a compiler is faster” — explain why: no run-time translation means the executable runs without the overhead of translating each line.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Low-level languages (machine code, assembly language) are close to hardware: fast and precise but hard to read, not portable, and processor-specific. High-level languages (e.g. Python) use English-like syntax, are portable across hardware, and are far easier to write and debug.
  • A compiler translates the entire program into machine code before execution, producing a standalone executable. Errors are all reported after analysis. Once compiled, no translator is needed to run the program.
  • An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time during execution. It stops at the first error (easy to locate) but is slower than compiled code and the interpreter must be present every time the program runs.

practice_questions.text: Define the term high-level programming language.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: a programming language that uses English-like syntax (1 mark) and is portable across different processor types, providing a high level of abstraction from hardware (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a compiler translates a high-level language program.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: a compiler reads and translates the entire program (1 mark) into machine code in one pass before execution, producing a standalone executable file (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between a compiler and an interpreter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two of the following, each with justification. (1) Translation timing: a compiler translates the whole program before execution; an interpreter translates one statement at a time during execution. This means compiled code runs faster because no run-time translation is needed. (2) Output: a compiler produces a standalone machine code executable; an interpreter does not — the interpreter must be present every time the program runs. (3) Error reporting: a compiler reports all errors after analysing the whole program; an interpreter stops at the first error encountered, making the error location immediately clear. Each difference must include an explanation of the consequence or reason, not just a bare contrast.
Secure: Two differences stated correctly with some justification for each.
Developing: Two differences stated without justification, or one difference with justification.
Emerging: One difference stated with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Give one advantage of using assembly language rather than machine code.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: assembly language uses readable mnemonics (e.g. MOV, ADD) instead of binary, making it easier to read and write than machine code. Accept any reference to readability, human-readable codes, or the use of mnemonics.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage of using a high-level language rather than a low-level language when developing software for a school attendance management system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: High-level languages use English-like syntax (e.g. Python), making the code much easier to read and understand. In a team environment, other developers can maintain or extend the system without needing to understand the underlying hardware architecture. Additionally, high-level languages are portable — the attendance system could be deployed on different hardware (Windows servers, Linux servers) without rewriting the code. Programmes can also be written and debugged much faster.
Secure: States one advantage clearly (e.g. easier to read, portable) and links it to the scenario.
Developing: States an advantage of high-level languages without linking to the school context.
Emerging: Vague reference to high-level being easier.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using an interpreter compared to a compiler for a developer who is writing and testing a new program. In your answer, consider both the development phase and the final product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During development, an interpreter is advantageous: it translates and runs one line at a time, stopping immediately at the first error and showing exactly which line failed, giving fast feedback. No compilation step is needed before each test run. However, once the program is finished, interpreted code runs more slowly than compiled code because translation happens at run time. The interpreter must also be installed on every machine that runs the program, adding a dependency. A compiler is slower to use during development (the whole program must be compiled before testing), but produces a standalone executable that runs faster and does not require the compiler to be present. Concludes: interpreters are more convenient during development; compilers produce better final products.
Secure: Identifies interpreter’s advantage for error location during development and compiler’s advantage for speed and standalone execution; some evaluation of trade-offs.
Developing: Describes one advantage of each without evaluating the development vs deployment distinction.
Emerging: Simple statements about one translator with little comparison.

glossary_terms.definition: Binary instructions (patterns of 0s and 1s) that can be executed directly by a processor. Each processor family has its own specific machine code instruction set.
Programming languages that are close to machine code and provide little or no abstraction from hardware. Machine code and assembly language are both low-level languages.
A low-level programming language that uses short text codes called mnemonics (e.g. MOV, ADD) to represent machine code instructions, with a one-to-one correspondence.
Programming languages that use English-like syntax and are portable across different types of processor, providing a high level of abstraction from hardware.
A translator that converts an entire high-level language program into machine code in one pass before execution, producing a standalone executable file.

A translator that converts and executes a high-level program one statement at a time during execution, without producing a standalone executable. The interpreter must be present every time the program runs.
